outline.description: Introduces the parties, the competing marks and services, and traces the matter from Apex’s intent-to-use applications through the TTAB opposition and the Federal Circuit appeal.
subtopics: Parties and marks: CC Serve’s ASPIRE (Reg. No. 2126948; priority October 17, 1996) for credit card services; Apex Bank’s planned ASPIRE BANK word and design marks for banking and financing services

Nature of services: CC Serve partners with issuing banks to offer ASPIRE-branded credit cards and services; Apex is a Tennessee retail bank with no current credit card offerings, planning an internet bank under ASPIRE BANK
USPTO prosecution: 2019 intent-to-use filings; CC Serve’s letter of protest; examining attorney approval; publication
TTAB proceeding: Section 2(d) opposition filed by CC Serve; Board sustains opposition for likelihood of confusion
Appeal: Apex appeals to the Federal Circuit; jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(4)(B); issues raised on appeal (errors in DuPont factors 2, 6, and 1)

outline.description: Sets out the legal framework for Section 2(d) likelihood-of-confusion analysis, the DuPont factors, and the standards of review that shape the Federal Circuit’s assessment of the TTAB decision.
subtopics: Section 2(d) of the Lanham Act: refusal of registration where concurrent use is likely to cause confusion
DuPont framework: thirteen non-exhaustive factors; Board need consider only those relevant and of record
Standard of review: legal conclusions de novo; each DuPont factor is a factual finding reviewed for substantial evidence
Second DuPont factor (relatedness of goods/services): products/services need not be identical; relatedness and marketing circumstances sufficient to create source confusion
Sixth DuPont factor (number and nature of similar marks): third-party use and registrations on similar goods/services can show commercial weakness and a crowded field

First DuPont factor (similarity of the marks): comparison in their entireties for appearance, sound, connotation, and commercial impression; commercial impression can be influenced by marketplace strength/weakness

outline.chapter_title: Factor Two: Similarity of Services and the Board’s Affirmed Determination
outline.description: Details the Board’s analysis concluding that Apex’s identified services are highly similar—and in part legally identical—to CC Serve’s, and explains why the Federal Circuit affirmed.
subtopics: Defining CC Serve’s identified services: Board construes deleted ID Manual term “credit card services” to include issuing cards, processing transactions, authorization, account management, alerts/monitoring, and access to credit scores
Dictionary definitions: “bank,” “banking,” and “finance” encompass extending credit, including by issuing credit cards
Overlap finding: Apex’s “banking and financing services” are legally identical in part to CC Serve’s “credit card services”
Third-party registrations: evidence that entities commonly offer both credit card and broader banking/financing services under a single mark
Board’s conclusion: high degree of similarity; factor two weighs heavily for CC Serve
Apex’s counterarguments and their rejection: non-identity and non-competition; CC Serve is not itself a bank; Apex does not offer credit cards; identification-of-services controls the analysis
Federal Circuit holding: substantial evidence supports the Board’s finding; no legal error; factor two affirmed

outline.chapter_title: Factor Six: Third-Party Use, the Board’s Legal Error, and Remand Instructions
outline.description: Explains why the Board’s narrowing of the relevant marketplace to only credit card services was legally erroneous under factor six and what the Federal Circuit requires on remand.
subtopics: Board’s approach: limited relevant public to consumers of credit card services; discounted Aspire-formative uses for other banking/financing services as “essentially irrelevant”
Board’s evidentiary finding: nine Aspire-formative marks for credit card services; deemed insufficient to show a “considerable” or “ubiquitous” level of use

Legal error identified: factor six does not require identical goods/services; where factor two finds services highly similar (even legally identical in part), the same breadth of similarity must inform factor six
Consistency principle: maintain the similarity scope used under factor two when evaluating other DuPont factors, including factor six
Remand directive: reconsider factor six by including third-party marks used on similar banking and financing services (not just credit card services) and reassess the commercial strength of ASPIRE
Doctrinal significance: proper treatment of crowded-field evidence; third-party use across similar (not only identical) financial services can narrow the mark’s scope of protection

outline.chapter_title: Factor One, Interdependence of Factors, and Disposition
outline.description: Shows how factor one’s commercial impression analysis depends on the mark’s strength under factor six, and sets out the court’s ultimate disposition and practical implications.
subtopics: Interdependence: commercial impression under factor one is informed by marketplace strength/weakness developed under factor six
Vacatur of factor one: because re-evaluating factor six may alter the perceived strength of ASPIRE, the Board’s factor-one analysis must be reconsidered

Scope of reconsideration: compare ASPIRE and ASPIRE BANK (word and design) in their entireties—appearance, sound, connotation, and commercial impression—taking into account any revised strength findings
Outcome: affirmed-in-part (factor two), vacated-in-part (factors six and one), remanded for further proceedings; costs to appellant
Key takeaways: keep the similarity scope consistent across DuPont factors; build robust records of third-party use on similar services; identifications of services drive the analysis before the TTAB
